articles.title: Your first 90 days after the uniform: a calm checklist
articles.why: Breaks the overwhelm of separation into small, doable steps so you can prioritize without panic.
body: Leaving the service is a mission of its own — and like any mission, it goes better with a plan you can actually follow. This sample guide focuses on the first three months: paperwork that unlocks benefits, a simple budget, and connecting with people who have already walked the path.

Start with identity documents, DD-214 copies, and enrolling in VA health care if you are eligible. Next, map housing, income, and any family needs. You do not have to do everything in week one. Pick three priorities and finish those before stacking more.

Many veterans find that talking to a peer mentor or a local nonprofit coordinator shortens the learning curve. South Carolina partners like Upstate Warrior Solution and Vantage Point Foundation exist for exactly this kind of practical navigation. Ask for help early — it is strength, not weakness.
Remember: transition is not a single day. Give yourself patience, sleep, and room to miss the camaraderie while you build a new rhythm at home.

articles.title: Translating military skills into civilian job language
articles.why: Helps you rewrite your experience so hiring managers understand your value without the jargon.
body: Civilian résumés reward clarity, not acronyms. When you led a squad, you managed people, deadlines, and risk. When you maintained equipment, you owned quality, safety, and uptime. This sample piece walks through swapping military titles for outcomes.

Try the formula: action + responsibility + result. Example: instead of “NCOIC of logistics cell,” write “Coordinated supply for 120 personnel, cutting wait times by streamlining inventory checks.” Numbers help — even rough ones.
Practice saying your story out loud in two minutes. Friends and family can catch jargon you no longer notice. Career centers and veteran employment programs often offer free résumé reviews; use them.
You already have leadership, discipline, and composure under pressure. The job is packaging that so someone outside the wire can see it.

articles.title: When sleep won’t come: small steps that often help
articles.why: Offers gentle, practical sleep hygiene ideas — and clear pointers to professional and crisis care when needed.
body: Sleep problems are common after service. Hypervigilance, irregular schedules, and stress do not shut off overnight. This sample article is not medical advice; it shares habits many veterans find useful while encouraging professional care when sleep loss is severe.

Keep a consistent wake time, even after a rough night. Dim screens an hour before bed. Avoid caffeine late in the day. If racing thoughts show up, keep a notepad nearby — write the worry down and tell yourself you will handle it in daylight.

If nightmares, mood swings, or thoughts of self-harm are part of the picture, reach out. The Veterans Crisis Line is available 24/7: dial 988 then press 1, or text 838255. You are not alone, and help is real.
Peer support groups and VA mental health clinics can pair well with everyday habits. Healing is not linear — progress counts even when it is quiet.

articles.title: Talking with your kids about what deployment meant
articles.why: Gives age-aware conversation starters so families reconnect without forcing a single “perfect” talk.
body: Kids notice absence and change even when they cannot name it. Coming home — or starting a civilian chapter — is a chance to rebuild trust through small, honest moments rather than one big speech.

For younger children, keep it simple and reassuring: you left to do an important job, you are safe now, and you love them. For teens, invite questions and accept that some days they may not want to talk. Presence matters more than perfect answers.
Shared routines help: a weekly walk, cooking together, or a standing game night. Partners need check-ins too — reintegration is a family mission.
If tension stays high, counselors who understand military culture can help. Asking for support models strength for your children.

articles.title: GI Bill basics without the maze
articles.why: Skims the essentials so you can ask sharper questions at a school or VA education office.
body: Education benefits can feel like alphabet soup. This sample overview covers the big ideas: eligibility depends on your service dates and character of discharge; benefits may include tuition, housing stipends, and book allowances; and deadlines and school approvals matter.

Before you enroll, confirm your Certificate of Eligibility and whether your school participates. Compare programs by outcome — not just ads. Certificate programs, community college, and trade schools can be excellent fits alongside four-year degrees.
Keep copies of every form. If something looks wrong on a payment, call early. Veteran school certifying officials are there to help; so are accredited representatives through VSO organizations.
Education is one path among many. Pair schooling with career goals so the benefit serves your next chapter, not the other way around.

articles.title: “I still check the exits”: a veteran’s story of finding steady ground
articles.why: A relatable peer story that normalizes hypervigilance and shows that connection and routine can help.
body: Marcus sat with his back to the wall in every restaurant for two years after he got out. He told himself it was just habit. His wife noticed. His kids noticed. He pretended not to.

What changed was not a sudden cure. It was a weekly coffee with two other veterans, a counselor who did not flinch at his jokes, and a job that valued his calm under pressure. The exits still get a glance — but the glance no longer runs the whole meal.
This is a sample story, written for this prototype. Real veterans’ stories are sacred; we share a composite to show the tone we aim for: honest, hopeful, never preachy.
If Marcus’s habits sound familiar, consider peer groups, mentoring programs, or a local retreat space. Places like Semper Fi Barn exist so veterans can reset among people who get it.

articles.title: Networking without the awkward elevator pitch
articles.why: Reframes networking as mutual help — something many service members already know how to do.
body: Networking sounds fake until you remember the military runs on relationships. You already know how to look out for your people. Civilian networking is the same skill in softer clothes.
Start with warm contacts: former leaders, unit mates, neighbors, church or gym communities, and local veteran nonprofits. Ask for advice, not a job. People like being useful.
Bring a short story about what you are good at and what you are looking for. Follow up with a thank-you. Offer help back when you can — introductions, volunteering, or sharing a resource.
Chambers of commerce, hiring events, and organizations like Vantage Point Foundation’s leadership programs can open doors you will not find on a job board alone.

articles.title: Disability claim myths that waste time
articles.why: Clears up common misconceptions so you can prepare evidence and get accredited help sooner.
body: Myth one: “If I file, I am taking from someone else.” Benefits you earned are not charity. Myth two: “I need a lawyer on day one.” Many veterans start with accredited VSOs at no cost. Myth three: “Buddy statements do not matter.” Lay evidence can strengthen a claim when records are thin.

Gather service treatment records, private medical notes, and a clear list of conditions tied to service. Be honest about severity — exaggeration hurts credibility; underplaying can leave you under-supported.
Timelines vary. Appeals exist for a reason. Keep organized folders, digital or paper. Ask questions until you understand the next step.
This sample is educational, not legal advice. For your claim, talk with an accredited representative or VA.

articles.title: Partners reintegrating: rebuilding the team at home
articles.why: Normalizes the bumpiness of coming home and offers couple-focused check-in habits.
body: You both changed. That is normal. Roles that worked during deployment may need renegotiating — chores, money, parenting, quiet time. Resentment grows in silence; curiosity shrinks it.
Try a weekly 20-minute check-in: What went well? What was hard? What do you need from me this week? Keep phones away. Listen to understand, not to win.
Intimacy and friendship rebuild at different speeds. Patience is not indifference — it is strategy. If fights escalate or safety feels shaky, seek counseling promptly.
Many couples thrive after service. The ones who do often treat reintegration like a shared mission with clear communication and outside support when needed.

articles.title: Horses, hay, and healing: why equine programs click for some veterans
articles.source: Eden Farms / Happy Hooves program note (sample)
articles.why: Introduces equine-assisted approaches as one option among many — grounded, sensory, and community-based.
body: Not every veteran wants a fluorescent waiting room. Working alongside horses asks for calm presence, clear cues, and respect — skills that transfer from service and invite the nervous system to settle.

Programs near Greenville, including Eden Farms and Happy Hooves, focus on connection with animals and open land. This sample note describes the vibe, not a clinical claim: many participants report feeling more grounded after consistent sessions.
Equine work is not a replacement for therapy when therapy is needed. It can sit beside counseling, peer groups, or medical care as another tool in the kit.
If barns and trails sound like your kind of reset, ask local coordinators about veteran-focused offerings and how to get started.

articles.title: Finding your people after the unit
articles.why: Reminds you that belonging is rebuildable — through peers, hobbies, faith, and local veteran spaces.
body: The hardest part of getting out is often not the paperwork. It is the sudden quiet where your team used to be. Belonging does not vanish permanently — it needs new soil.

Look for low-pressure contact: a weekly workout with other veterans, a volunteer shift, a faith community, a hobby meetup, or a case-coordination nonprofit that also builds community. Upstate Warrior Solution and similar groups often know where people gather.
You do not owe anyone your war stories. Shared purpose — fixing something, cooking, hiking, mentoring — rebuilds trust sideways.
Loneliness is common and treatable with connection. Reach out before the silence gets loud. Crisis support is always available at 988 then 1 if you are in acute distress.

articles.title: A weekend to reset: what retreat spaces can offer
articles.why: Points to restorative time offline — useful when daily life feels crowded and loud.
body: Sometimes the bravest move is stepping away for a quiet weekend. Retreat spaces designed for veterans offer rest without performance — no need to be “on,” just present.

Semper Fi Barn, near Six Mile and Central in South Carolina, is one such place in this prototype’s partner set: barns, open air, and room to breathe. Details and availability live on their site; this sample simply names the idea.
Pair a retreat with follow-through at home: one habit, one person you will call, one appointment you will keep. Reset is a beginning, not a finish line.
If cost or logistics are barriers, ask — many veteran-serving organizations help with access.

articles.title: Contact a local VSO: Upstate SC county Veterans Affairs Officers
articles.why: Explains what a Veterans Service Officer does and how to reach county CVAOs in Pickens, Greenville, Anderson, and Oconee — with real SCDVA links.
body: Sample guidance for Warrior Wayfinder™: you do not have to file a VA claim alone. A Veterans Service Officer (often called a VSO rep) or your County Veterans Affairs Officer (CVAO) is an accredited helper who can prepare claims, gather evidence, track status, and — when needed — guide appeals. County offices in South Carolina generally provide this help at no charge to the veteran.

What a VSO / CVAO typically does: reviews your DD-214 and medical history, helps you describe conditions tied to service, submits forms correctly, and keeps you from common filing mistakes. They are not a substitute for your doctor, but they know how the claims process works. Bring copies of service and medical records, a list of conditions, and questions written down.

Upstate starting points (verify hours before you go): Greenville County Veterans Affairs — greenvillecounty.org/VeteranAffairs/ (County Square, Greenville; main line often listed via SCDVA). Anderson County Veterans Affairs — andersoncountysc.org departments page for Veterans Affairs (appointment-based). Pickens and Oconee CVAOs are listed on the SCDVA County Veterans’ Affairs Offices directory — use that page for current names, phones, and emails, because staff change.

Statewide hub: scdva.sc.gov/county-resources lists every SC county’s Veterans Affairs Officer, with phone and email. SCDVA Benefits & Claims (scdva.sc.gov/benefits-claims) explains how county offices and state staff work together. Federally, VA.gov’s accredited representative search finds VSOs, attorneys, and claims agents. SC Smart Start (scdvasmartstart.sc.gov) helps with broader transition questions.
This article is educational sample content — not legal advice. For your claim, work with an accredited representative or the VA. If you are in crisis, dial 988 then press 1.

articles.title: Family life in the Upstate: events, orgs, and military discounts
articles.why: Points families to local Upstate events and orgs, plus stores with official veteran discount programs and the IDs that prove you served.
body: Sample article for demo: rebuilding family rhythm after service is easier when you know where to gather and where a military ID still opens a door. Start with people and places — discounts are a bonus, not the plan.

Family-friendly connection: check the in-app Events calendar for verified Upstate gatherings (peer groups, Legion fellowship, community salutes, and outdoor retreats). Confirm dates and RSVP on the organization’s site. Happy Hooves at Eden Farms (Marietta) offers equine programs that many families find calming. Military OneSource remains a strong national option for confidential counseling and parenting tools.

Local orgs that help families: Upstate Warrior Solution coordinates practical help across Greenville, Anderson, Pickens, Spartanburg, and Oconee. Semper Fi Barn near Six Mile welcomes veterans and families for fellowship. Vantage Point Foundation supports post-9/11 transition statewide with Upstate presence. Browse the Orgs tab for homepage links.

Veteran discounts (terms change, so check the source): Lowe’s publishes Military Discount Program terms that include veterans and spouses (lowes.com/pdf/Military_Discount_Program_Terms.pdf). The Home Depot explains how veterans sign up for its military discount on its own site (corporate.homedepot.com). Target’s military discount for veterans shows up during its military campaigns, not every day. Most stores ask for proof — VA lists the IDs that work, including the free digital Veteran ID Card (va.gov/records/get-veteran-id-cards/). The Benefits & discounts screen, at the top of the Orgs tab, links each of these.

Local shops and restaurants sometimes set their own veteran discounts, and those change often — ask at places you already like before you count on one. This piece is sample content, not a coupon guarantee.

articles.title: Veteran-friendly employers: Upstate SC and national options
articles.why: Lists real major employers known for Upstate presence or veteran hiring — with career links and a clear “check current openings” reminder.
body: Sample careers guide for Warrior Wayfinder™. Do not invent a “guaranteed hire” — look for employers with real footprint, published veteran programs, or SCDVA recognition, then check current openings yourself.

Upstate / South Carolina anchors: Michelin (North America HQ in Greenville; plants nearby) — jobs.michelinman.com. BMW Group Plant Spartanburg publicly highlights veteran hiring — bmwgroup.jobs Spartanburg location page. Lockheed Martin Greenville — aircraft work with a careers location page. Prisma Health — large regional health system careers site. GE Aerospace has veteran pathways (including SkillBridge at many sites); search Greenville/SC roles on their jobs site. Amazon runs national military recruiting pages and has logistics presence in the Carolinas.

Public sector & recognized lists: USAJOBS.gov for federal roles with veterans’ preference. SCDVA’s Recognized Veteran-Friendly Employers page highlights organizations (including Upstate examples such as Greenville-area public safety and Upstate Warrior Solution in past recognitions) — use it as a starting map, not a job board. County and city governments, SC National Guard technician jobs, and VA medical centers also hire regularly.

National programs that open doors: Hiring Our Heroes (U.S. Chamber), VA Veteran Readiness & Employment (Chapter 31), and corporate military recruiting hubs at defense and Fortune 500 firms. Pair these with the résumé and networking tips in our other Jobs articles.
Every link and name here is a lead, not a promise. Openings change weekly — always check current openings and never pay a recruiter who guarantees a federal or defense job. Sample content for demo.

articles.title: Hiring tips that work after the uniform
articles.why: Practical interview and application habits for veterans — pairs with the employer list and SkillBridge / VR&E paths.
body: Sample tips: treat your job search like a short campaign with weekly goals — applications sent, conversations held, skills practiced — not a single all-or-nothing push.
Lead with outcomes. Hiring managers skim. Open with the problem you solved, the team size, the tools, and the result. Keep a two-minute spoken version ready for interviews and networking events.

Use veteran pathways deliberately: SkillBridge (while still serving, if eligible), VR&E if you qualify, Hiring Our Heroes fellowships, and USAJOBS veterans’ preference. On corporate sites, search “military,” “veterans,” or “SkillBridge” career pages.

Ask for referrals inside companies that already employ veterans — BMW Spartanburg, Michelin, Lockheed Greenville, Prisma, and federal agencies often have employee resource groups. A warm intro beats a cold apply.

Follow up once, politely. Track applications in a simple spreadsheet. If you stall, book a résumé review through a VSO, SC Smart Start, or a local nonprofit coordinator. This is educational sample content, not placement advice.

articles.title: Pickens, Greenville, Anderson, Oconee: quick VSO contact map
articles.why: A short county-by-county reminder to use the official SCDVA directory — phones and officers change.
body: Sample quick-reference: South Carolina’s County Veterans Affairs Officers are your local front door for claims help. Always confirm the current officer, phone, and hours on scdva.sc.gov/county-resources before you drive.

Greenville: County Veterans Affairs at County Square (University Ridge) — public page at greenvillecounty.org/VeteranAffairs/. Anderson: county Veterans Affairs department page lists appointment-only claims help. Pickens and Oconee: use the SCDVA directory for the latest CVAO contact (staff names rotate).
Bring DD-214, ID, medical evidence, and a written list of claimed conditions. Ask whether they can also point you to SC Smart Start, housing, or employment partners if those are part of your plan.
Families: survivors and dependents can often get help with DIC and related benefits through the same offices. This sample card is not legal advice — accredited help matters.

articles.title: When housing is shaky: first calm calls in Upstate SC
articles.why: A gentle first-call map for emergency shelter, food, and VA housing help across Greenville, Pickens, and Oconee — verify hours before you go.
body: Sample guidance for Warrior Wayfinder™: if you are sleeping in a car, couch-surfing, facing eviction, or worried about tonight, you do not have to sort every program alone. Start with one or two calls, then let a coordinator help with the next steps.

Immediate local doors (verify hours and intake): The Salvation Army of Greenville, Pickens & Oconee Counties (salvationarmyusa.org Greenville SC Area Command) offers shelter, meals, and emergency assistance — call ahead. Our Daily Rest in Seneca (o365.ourdailyrest.org) serves Oconee with emergency and white-flag shelter; intake windows are limited. Clemson Community Care (clemsoncommunitycare.org) helps with food pantry, utilities, and homelessness support for the Clemson / Central / Pendleton area. United Way SC 211 (sc211.org or dial 2-1-1) is a statewide free referral line for shelter, food banks, and crisis resources.

Veteran-specific housing paths: VA Supportive Services for Veteran Families (SSVF) helps eligible Veteran families prevent or exit homelessness — start at department.va.gov/homeless (SSVF). Columbia VA Health Care for Homeless Veterans (HCHV) has Upstate outreach — va.gov Columbia homeless-veteran-care page. United Housing Connections leads the Upstate Continuum of Care (unitedhousingconnections.org / upstatecoc.org) and coordinates many shelter and rehousing partners, including veteran-focused efforts. SCDVA’s housing resources page (scdva.sc.gov/housing-resources) lists state-linked options.

Note on SC Serves: the AmericaServes SCServes Coordination Center is no longer operational (IVMF status page). Use 211, your County Veterans Affairs Officer, Upstate Warrior Solution, United Housing Connections, or VA homeless programs instead. This article is sample educational content — always verify hours, eligibility, and openings locally. If you are in crisis, dial 988 then press 1.

articles.title: Food, shelter, and the next overnight: a calm Upstate checklist
articles.why: Short checklist for pantry, shelter, and coordinated entry — pairs with the Housing resource cards in Browse.
body: Sample checklist: (1) Food tonight — Clemson Community Care pantry or Salvation Army Greenville food programs; ask 211 for the nearest open pantry. (2) Safe overnight — call Salvation Army Greenville Area Command or Our Daily Rest before you travel; white-flag / weather nights have different rules. (3) Tell someone you trust where you are.

(4) Veteran channel — ask for SSVF or HCHV through VA homeless programs, or call Upstate Warrior Solution for case coordination. (5) Paperwork later — DD-214 and ID help, but many shelters will still talk to you first on a hard night.

Coordinated entry through the Upstate Continuum of Care (United Housing Connections) is how many longer-term housing placements start. You do not need to memorize every acronym — one warm referral often unlocks the rest.
This is demo sample content, not a guarantee of a bed. Verify locally every time.

articles.title: Women veterans & spouses: where to get help without the runaround
articles.why: Points women veterans and military spouses to VA women’s health, Military OneSource, local UWS, childcare/benefits pointers, and a real SC women-vet community.
body: Sample article for Warrior Wayfinder™: women who served — and the spouses who kept the home front running — often get steered to generic “veteran” lines that miss women’s health, childcare, and spouse career needs. You deserve doors that already understand that.

Health & VA: Women Veterans Health Care (womenshealth.va.gov) covers gynecology, maternity coordination, mental health, and how to enroll. Columbia VA’s women veteran care page lists local women’s health services for much of SC, including Upstate catchment. The Women Veterans Call Center (listed on VA women’s health pages) can help you find a Women Veterans Program Manager.

Spouse & family support: Military OneSource (militaryonesource.mil) offers confidential counseling, spouse career tools, and parenting help 24/7. Their milspouse support pages and childcare program guides (including MCCYN/fee-assistance overviews) are solid starting points — eligibility depends on your status; verify on the site. Upstate Warrior Solution helps veterans and families with practical case coordination across Greenville, Anderson, Pickens, Spartanburg, and Oconee.

Community: She’s the Veteran (shestheveteran.org) is a South Carolina–rooted women veterans community (Charleston-based with statewide/virtual reach) — confirm current events on their site. Pair peer community with clinical care when you need both. This piece is educational sample content, not medical advice. Crisis: 988 then 1.

articles.title: A weekly virtual Talking Circle for Women Veterans
articles.why: A free, peer-led online circle built around women veterans’ experiences — no travel or child care to arrange.
body: VA News notes that women Veterans are the fastest-growing group in the Veteran population, yet many still hit everyday barriers to staying connected — a canceled appointment because child care fell through, not knowing travel help may be available, or not seeing their own experiences reflected in the room.

Televeda runs a free Virtual Talking Circle for Women Veterans as part of its Hero’s Story Project. Per the article it meets online every Tuesday at 3 p.m. Arizona time. Peers, not clinicians, lead the group; participants set the pace and share only what feels right. It is designed around women Veterans’ experiences, including survivors of military sexual trauma.

To join, reserve a spot through Televeda’s class schedule. Participants who want help applying for VA benefits or enrolling in VA health care can ask a facilitator for guidance. VA notes that sharing non-VA information is not an endorsement — confirm details with Televeda.

articles.title: Women Veterans: You deserve to be safe
articles.why: Plain-language help on intimate partner violence (IPV) and every door VA offers — any staff member, coordinators, and hotlines.
body: VA News reports that about one in three women Veterans experience intimate partner violence during their lives, and that women Veterans affected by IPV are three times more likely to face housing instability or homelessness. IPV can be physical, verbal, emotional, financial, or sexual abuse, or stalking, by a current or former partner.

VA uses a “no wrong door” approach. You can tell your VA health care or mental health provider or any VA staff member; contact your local IPV assistance program coordinator or women Veterans program manager; call the Veterans Crisis Line (988, then press 1, or text 838255); call the National Domestic Violence Hotline (800-799-7233); call or text the Women Veterans Call Center (855-829-6636); tell VA police; or call 911 for immediate help.
VA can also help connect you to community resources, including safety and escape planning. If you are in danger right now, call 911.

articles.title: Healthy aging for women Veterans: What you can do today for a stronger tomorrow
articles.why: A short checklist of screenings and conversations to have with your VA team as you age.
body: Written for Healthy Aging Month, this VA News piece lists areas women Veterans can focus on with their VA health care team. Bones: weight-bearing activity like walking helps, and you can ask whether a bone density test is right for you, especially once you are 65. Mammograms: average-risk women should start at age 40 — talk with your provider about your risks.

Gynecology still matters after menopause: most average-risk women start cervical cancer screening at 21, and you can schedule a pelvic exam or Pap test through VA. For mental health, the article points to VA mental health support and Vet Centers — small, non-medical counseling centers in the community.

It also covers memory and brain health (talk to your provider about changes and prepare legal and financial documents), menopause symptoms, and bladder and pelvic health, which it says are treatable — not just part of getting older.

articles.title: Navigating menopause with VA
articles.why: Explains the phases of menopause, why women Veterans may have earlier or stronger symptoms, and what VA can treat.
body: Menopause unfolds in three phases — perimenopause (often starting in your 40s), menopause (12 months without a period, most often in the early 50s), and post-menopause, when risks for heart disease, osteoporosis, and urinary incontinence rise.

VA News says women Veterans may experience earlier or more intense menopause because of military-related stressors and exposures: chronic stress, PTSD, trauma, and depression can disrupt hormones; smoking is linked to earlier menopause; and exposures like burn pits and chemicals may impair ovarian function.

Services you may be eligible for include hormonal and non-hormonal medications, sleep support, Whole Health options such as acupuncture, mental health support, lifestyle counseling, bone density testing, and therapies for vaginal and urinary symptoms, including pelvic floor physical therapy.

articles.title: Women’s Health Care Needs
articles.why: The official overview of what VA covers for women Veterans and the first two steps to get it.
body: If you qualify for VA health care, women’s health services are part of your benefits. Primary care includes disease prevention and nutrition counseling; reproductive health such as birth control, preconception counseling, and menopausal support; screenings like Pap smears and mammograms; mental health care for depression, PTSD, and substance use; and free, confidential care related to military sexual trauma.

Specialty services include managing chronic conditions like heart disease and diabetes, maternity care, treatment for urinary incontinence and sexual problems, prosthetic and sensory aids (including post-mastectomy items), rehabilitation referrals, and homebound and long-term care for those who qualify. Enrolled women Veterans can reach a VA provider by phone 24/7 through their local VA medical center.

To get started, apply for VA health care. After that, talk to your primary care provider, or contact the Women Veterans Program Manager at your local VA medical center to coordinate the services you need.

articles.title: Women Veterans Call Center
articles.why: One free, confidential number for any question about VA services for women — even if you never enrolled.
body: The Women Veterans Call Center helps you navigate VA, points you in the right direction, and connects you with the Women Veterans Program Manager at your local VA medical center. It is free and confidential, and you can call as many times as you need. A friend, relative, or caregiver can also call for you.

Call or text 1-855-VA-WOMEN (855-829-6636), or use the online chat on the Women Veterans Health Care site. Per the page, representatives are available Monday–Friday 8:00 a.m.–10:00 p.m. ET and Saturday 8:00 a.m.–6:30 p.m. ET, excluding federal holidays.

You do not need to be registered with VA or enrolled in VA health care, and you can use the call center with any discharge status. Example questions: reconnecting with VA care you applied for long ago, finding your local Maternity Care Coordinator or Women Veterans Program Manager, checking eligibility for benefits, and refilling a prescription or making an appointment.

articles.title: Maternity Care
articles.why: What VA covers through pregnancy, delivery, and postpartum — and how a Maternity Care Coordinator helps.
body: VA covers maternity care through pregnancy, delivery, and postpartum, and every VA facility offers maternity care coordination. VA Maternity Care Coordinators (MCCs) can answer questions about services and coverage at every stage of your pregnancy.

Coverage includes newborn care on the date of birth plus 7 days after. VA also covers nursing bras, breast/chest pumps, and maternity belts — request them through your MCC at least two weeks before your due date. Lactation pads, milk storage bags, and nipple cream are available through the VA Pharmacy.

Some services may not be covered, including home deliveries, doulas, and experimental procedures; your MCC can explain coverage. To find an MCC, contact your VA provider or local Women Veterans Program Manager.

articles.title: Military Sexual Trauma: Effects & Veteran Resources
articles.why: VA offers free, confidential MST-related care no matter how long ago it happened — plus a private self-help app.
body: VA uses the term military sexual trauma (MST) for sexual assault or sexual harassment experienced during military service — including being pressured or coerced into sexual activity, sexual contact without consent, or threatening comments about your body or sexual activities.

Anyone can experience MST, regardless of age, sex, sexual orientation, background, or branch. Like other trauma, it can affect mental and physical health many years later. VA provides free and confidential MST-related care to Veterans and other former service members, no matter how long ago the experience occurred.

The free Beyond MST mobile app has more than 30 tools to help survivors cope and manage symptoms. You do not need an account or to be in treatment, and VA says information you enter is not shared with anyone, including VA.

articles.title: Carrying the weight: Why caregiver well-being is part of suicide prevention
articles.why: For anyone supporting a Veteran through a hard stretch: the signs of burnout and why your own care matters.
body: If you are helping a Veteran through a hard time, VA News says you are already helping to prevent suicide — and your own well-being is part of that picture. Caregivers can take on the stress and even secondhand trauma of the people they support, sometimes called caregiver burnout.

Signs worth watching for: feeling exhausted no matter how much you rest, pulling away from friends, snapping at people you love, losing interest in things that used to bring joy, or regularly feeling like you are running on empty. Healthy sleep, staying connected to friends, and keeping hobbies that are just for you can help.

Eligible caregivers can receive mentoring, training, respite, and other support through VA’s Caregiver Support Program. The Veterans Crisis Line is free, confidential, and available 24/7: dial 988, then press 1.

articles.title: Free legal & financial planning assistance for VA caregivers
articles.why: Primary family caregivers in VA’s comprehensive program can get no-cost legal and financial planning help.
body: VA’s Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers (PCAFC) includes legal and financial planning services for injured Veterans and their primary family caregivers.

Per VA News, services include one-on-one support from a certified concierge, personalized legal and financial planning guidance, referrals to trusted attorneys, educational tools, and 24/7 website and phone support — covered at no cost to you.

It may help if you are not sure where to start with legal or financial questions, want help managing finances, or need guidance finding the right legal resources. The article links to VA’s Legal and Financial Planning page for next steps.

articles.title: Caregivers find support and services at VA
articles.why: Real caregivers describe how VA’s Caregiver Support Program — including respite care — helped them keep going.
body: Caregivers can be family members managing medications, close friends driving a Veteran to appointments, or a neighbor helping with groceries. VA’s Caregiver Support Program (CSP) offers education, emotional support, and community so caregivers can look after themselves while caring for their Veteran.

The article follows Ron, who quit his job and moved in to care for his father, Lee, a World War II pilot, after Lee broke his hip. CSP connected Ron with resources including respite care — short-term relief that lets caregivers take a break, run errands, or travel — and a nurse on his caregiver support team helped him navigate VA health care.

Caregivers have a VA caregiver support team, and VA offers skills training, peer mentoring, and coaching, as well as the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers for those who qualify.

articles.title: VA’s Virtual Psychotherapy Program for Caregivers
articles.why: Free virtual therapy — individual, group, and couples/family — for caregivers in VA’s comprehensive caregiver program.
body: VA’s Caregiver Support Program launched the Virtual Psychotherapy Program for Caregivers (VPPC) for caregivers participating in the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers (PCAFC). Sessions happen by telehealth, so there is no travel.
The program includes individual therapy, group therapy, and couples/family therapy aimed at family dynamics and strengthening relationships. Sessions are confidential and tailored to each caregiver.

Interested PCAFC caregivers can reach out to their local Caregiver Support Program team (found with VA’s locator tool), which can start a referral. Caregivers can also call the Caregiver Support Line at 1-855-260-3274.

articles.title: VA Benefits For Family And Caregivers
articles.why: VA’s one-page map of benefits for spouses, children, survivors, and caregivers.
body: As the spouse or dependent child of a Veteran or service member, you may qualify for benefits including health care, life insurance, or money for school. Survivors may qualify for added benefits such as help with burial costs and survivor compensation. If you care for a Veteran, you may be eligible for support to help you care for the Veteran — and yourself.

The page links out by need: health care through CHAMPVA and caregiver support (training, counseling, and payments); Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (D.I.C.), Survivors Pension, and Aid and Attendance or Housebound benefits; education through Chapter 35 (DEA), the Fry Scholarship, and transferred Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits; and VA-backed home loans.
If you are worried about a Veteran in crisis, the Veterans Crisis Line is free, private, and available 24/7: call 988, text 838255, or start a confidential chat.

articles.title: CHAMPVA Benefits
articles.why: Health coverage for some spouses, children, and survivors of Veterans with permanent and total service-connected disabilities.
body: CHAMPVA (Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs) provides health care benefits to certain spouses, dependents, and survivors. You may be eligible if you are the spouse or dependent child of a Veteran rated permanently and totally disabled from a service-connected disability, or the surviving spouse or child of a Veteran who died from a service-connected disability or was rated permanently and totally disabled at death.
In certain cases, surviving spouses or children of service members who died in the line of duty may also qualify. If you are eligible for or enrolled in TRICARE, you cannot get CHAMPVA.

For newborns, VA cannot pay claims until the child is enrolled — get the child a Social Security number, add them as the Veteran’s dependent, then apply as soon as possible. The page also explains how remarriage can affect benefits.

articles.title: Survivors’ And Dependents’ Educational Assistance
articles.why: Chapter 35 (DEA) can help eligible spouses and children pay for school or job training.
body: If you are the child or spouse of a Veteran or service member who has died, is captured or missing, or is permanently and totally disabled due to a service-connected disability, you may be eligible for the Survivors’ and Dependents’ Educational Assistance (DEA) program, also called Chapter 35.

DEA can help pay for school or cover expenses while you train for a job. The Veteran or service member must meet one of several conditions — for example, being permanently and totally disabled from a service-connected disability or having died as a result of one.

The page notes rules to check before you start: if you receive Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (D.I.C.) as a child, you’ll need to give up those payments when you begin using DEA, and there are age and timing rules for children. Read the full eligibility details on VA.gov.

articles.title: In Afghanistan, I Put the Mission Ahead of Everything — Even a Lump in My Breast
articles.why: An Army nurse’s first-person account of putting everyone else first — and learning that recovery is not a failure to serve.
body: While deployed to Afghanistan, Army nurse Ellen Schimmels found a lump in her breast. Not wanting to disrupt operations or her teammates’ leave, she kept caring for service members and told no one for months, until a friend convinced her to get it checked. An ultrasound found a solid mass, and she was evacuated.

She writes about how teamwork and selflessness — and a lifelong habit of people-pleasing — had slowly turned into self-silencing. During treatment she struggled to accept that focusing on her recovery was not a failure to serve.
After treatment and a miscarriage, she conceived through IVF and had a daughter. She retired after more than 22 years in the Army and now teaches nurse practitioners and treats veterans.

articles.title: I Was a Homeless Woman Veteran. The Programs Meant to Help Weren’t Built for Survivors Like Me
articles.why: A Navy veteran’s first-person account of homelessness and the shortage of safe, women-only housing. Content note: describes sexual assault.
body: Tashandra Poullard served nearly a decade in the Navy, then worked as a cybersecurity contractor. After losing her job and her savings, she was denied housing assistance and ended up couch-surfing and moving back in with her parents. She writes that she was often mistaken at VA for a veteran’s spouse.

As a survivor of sexual assault, she refused co-ed shelters but couldn’t find gender-specific transitional housing; a women-only shelter she was referred to served domestic violence survivors and had no beds. She describes a homeless system “not designed with women veterans in mind.”

A stay at a Houston residence eventually qualified her for a federal housing voucher. She went on to earn a master’s in creative writing and now works as a visual journalist in Kentucky, where she is making a documentary about a shelter for homeless women veterans. Content note: the full essay describes sexual assault.

articles.title: The story of Marine Corps Veteran Esther Castañeda
articles.why: The first woman to go to the rifle range at Camp Pendleton — and a lifetime of stepping into new territory since.
body: When Esther Castañeda arrived at Camp Pendleton in 1979, she wanted the same chance to train as the Marines around her but was denied because she was a woman. When a colonel finally gave her the opportunity, she became the first woman to go to the rifle range there — and earned her Rifle Expert Badge.

She served three years on active duty and three in the reserve, working in supply and as a forklift operator. Afterward she drove a truck for FedEx, completed the LAPD Reserve Academy, rides a Harley-Davidson Sportster, and is learning woodturning through a VA woodworking class in Long Beach.
Today she feeds people experiencing homelessness in her community, and she says VA mental health and medical care have supported her well-being since leaving the military.

articles.title: From Afghanistan to Athlete – Kirstie Ennis conquers adversity and extreme sports
articles.why: A Marine helicopter gunner injured in a crash turns to snowboarding, mountaineering, and helping other adaptive athletes.
body: Kirstie Ennis enlisted in the Marine Corps at 17 and served as a door gunner and airframes mechanic on the CH-53 helicopter. In June 2012, during her second Afghanistan deployment, her helicopter crash-landed in Helmand Province. After about 40 surgeries over three years, her left leg was amputated.

Without a sports background, she took up snowboarding and won a USA Snowboard and Freeski Association national title. She set out to climb the Seven Summits; on Mount Kilimanjaro she left the dog tags of a friend killed in Afghanistan and became the first female above-the-knee amputee to summit it.
She started a nonprofit supporting education, sits on charity boards, and learned to build her own climbing prosthetics — then made a climbing foot for another veteran.

articles.title: A Military Man Straight Out of Central Casting. I Got to Know ‘Dadmiral’ in His Final Days
articles.source: The War Horse · Susan Macke Miller
articles.why: A daughter caring for her father, a retired Navy admiral, finds the man behind the armor in his last weeks.
body: Susan Macke Miller admired her father, a Navy admiral and former test pilot, mostly from a distance — his career and her parents’ divorce meant she saw him in childhood summers and at milestones. At 61, she cared for him as he was dying of cancer.

In those final weeks, she writes, “the warrior retired his armor and revealed his humanity.” He shared wishes, regrets, and untold stories, and she read aloud the 35 pages of memories he had typed for his grandsons — including flying 43 different aircraft.
She describes hard moments of caregiving alongside unexpected tenderness at his bedside — moments that “ruined me in the best way.”

articles.title: War Taught Me to Read a Room. My PTSD Service Dog Does It Better
articles.why: A Marine veteran on living with cumulative PTSD — and how his service dog, Blue, turned dependence into partnership.
body: Robert Macpherson spent 25 years in the Marines and then two decades in humanitarian and human rights work in places like Bosnia, Rwanda, Iraq, and Afghanistan. He describes his PTSD as cumulative — showing up as constant scanning, withdrawal, anger, and private shame over needing help.

Blue, a yellow Labrador trained as a PTSD service dog, has been beside him for nearly nine years. Blue threads him through crowds, nudges him out of nightmares, and once rested his head on his knee in a hospital waiting room before Macpherson had admitted the room was getting to him.

For someone who believed survival required self-reliance, he writes, depending on another creature did not come easily — but over time “dependence stopped feeling like weakness and began to feel like a partnership.”

articles.title: A chance conversation put this Navy Veteran on the path to franchise ownership
articles.why: How one Navy flight officer researched a franchise before buying — practical steps any veteran can copy.
body: Navy Veteran Nick Hernandez-Sepper served eight years as a naval flight officer, then worked in finance for defense contractors. Wanting to leave a desk job and have more time with his family, he learned about a painting franchise through a chance conversation with a friend.

Before committing, he reviewed the franchise disclosure document, which details fees, startup costs, training, support, and obligations. VA News notes that an independent franchise attorney and accountant can help evaluate it. He also called current owners — many of them veterans — and asked what surprised them and whether they would buy again.

He says the franchise playbook felt familiar after military service: “The systems allow you to sit in that captain’s chair and make those decisions.” VA notes that sharing non-VA information is not an endorsement.

articles.title: Richard DeLeon: Return from the Edge
articles.why: A Vietnam combat medic who struggled to readjust — and believes that seeking help made him a better man.
body: Drafted in 1968, New Yorker Richard DeLeon trained as a medic and chose Vietnam, serving with Company A, 1st Battalion, 12th Cavalry Regiment. Wounded by grenade shrapnel during an ambush, he spent the night treating the wounded until he ran out of bandages; 35 of the 40 men were wounded.
He later ran to a downed helicopter under fire to help free a surviving soldier and recover the dead.

After leaving the Army in 1970, he had trouble readjusting, feeling that great resources had prepared men for war but none helped them come home. He eventually found work on Wall Street and sought help — and today, VA News reports, he believes that seeking help made him a better man.

articles.title: Salvatore Giunta: Selfless brotherhood
articles.why: The first living Medal of Honor recipient since Vietnam — who says he did what any other soldier would have done.
body: Salvatore Giunta enlisted in the Army at 17 after seeing a recruitment commercial while working at a Subway in Iowa. On October 25, 2007, in Afghanistan’s Korengal Valley, his squad was ambushed from all directions during a night patrol.

Giunta ran into fire to reach his squad leader, was hit twice, and kept fighting to reach wounded friends. When he saw two insurgents dragging away his best friend, Sgt. Josh Brennan, he ran toward them; one insurgent was killed and the other dropped Brennan and fled, and Giunta kept the badly wounded Brennan alive while waiting for evacuation. Brennan died in surgery the next day.

In 2010 he became the first living recipient of the Medal of Honor since the Vietnam War. VA News reports he was not at peace with the award, believing he did what any other soldier would have done. He left the Army in 2011 to study at Colorado State University.
